item.title: What skills do you need to work in a hedge fund?
item.description:
The hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> industry is made up of a wide array of firms employing people with a wide array of skills. If you're a portfolio manager </news/finance/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund-lifestyle> it helps to be able to generate consistent profits with a Sharpe ratio (which measures risk adjusted returns) well above 1.5, but this isn't the only requirement. There is no single perfect candidate for hedge fund jobs, but you can get an idea of which skills are desired the most by listening to the top hedge fund managers, and by speaking to the recruiters that actually put candidates in front of them.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
What skills do hedge fund managers like?
Ken Griffin, </news/2023/10/citadel-goldman-sachs-114>CEO of Citadel, has spoken at length about the skills which his best employees possess. Speaking to the London School of Economics in 2024, he said that "one thing that always matters to us at Citadel is communication skills," and a willingness to debate. Citadel's people "argue their points with intensity, backed up by data;" Griffin said that doing this requires "deep thinking" and, while mathematical analysis can be useful to get your point across, it shouldn't be treated as a "crutch." Speaking at Stanford's 2026 Leadership Forum, Griffin said that "the success in your career will be defined as to whether or not you're a lifelong learner."
Dmitry Balyasny, </news/balyasny-hedge-fund> CEO of Balyasny Asset Management, appreciates "investment discipline." Speaking on a podcast <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O1M8y4QybU8>in February 2026, he said investment staff who "fall in love with one idea" but don't interrogate it or consider other possibilities will struggle. Balyasny also likes "passion." He said that being in the right role at the right firm is important to help you get past those "miserable periods when nothing is working [and] you feel like the biggest idiot in the world."
Steve Cohen, </news/point72-ceo-steve-cohen-it-s-better-to-look-stupid-than-be-mediocre> founder of Point72, similarly believes you need to have passion for the role; he also said in 2024 that you need to be in a "constant state of improvement." This requires humility, and a willingness to ask the "exceptional" people around you as many questions as you can. Cohen said he's "not afraid to look stupid" when doing so.
Ryan Tolkin, </news/hedge-fund-schonfeld-s-ceo-suggests-ai-will-mostly-eliminate-data-jobs?utm_source=chatgpt.com> CEO of Schonfeld, said on a podcast <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-S_S4tYymjk>in December that it's important to "escalate risk" and "speak up to share a perspective that might not be easily surfaced" by other members of a group. He said he built the culture at Schonfeld around this notion, and said that everyone, including junior staff, should be able to "challenge the norm [and] speak up."
Hamza Lemssouger, </news/hamza-lemssouguer-arini> CEO of Arini Capital, told students at the LSE Alternative Investments Conference this year that working in a hedge fund requires "discipline. It's about waking up every day, doing the same things and then keeping it and improving it." He said you need to be a professional pessimist in order to understand the risks of the actions you take; "you can be optimistic in life and pessimistic in work," he said.
What skills do you need to get a graduate job in a hedge fund?
It can be difficult to demonstrate all the traits above when you're so early into your career; hedge funds have ways around that.
In January, Citadel created a 'head of assessments' role for McKinsey consultant Keith McNulty </news/hedge-fund-citadel-hired-a-ph-d-talent-scientist-from-mc-kinsey>, who will be developing tests designed to assess the personality traits of graduate hires. Balyasny <https://www.businessinsider.com/inside-the-hedge-fund-hiring-frenzy-career-ladder-talent-wars-2026-2>uses similar tests to match interns with existing employees who can mentor them.
There are many ways to demonstrate discipline and competitiveness outside of a standardized test. For technical roles, like quant and engineering internships, participation in mathematics olympiads </news/networking-for-1m-quant-and-ai-jobs-really-begins-at-14-years-old>, hackathons, or other competitions can aid your chances. For non-technical roles, you could benefit more from being an athlete; Josh King, ex-head of corporate affairs at Citadel, said last summer that the fund has a "large collection of lacrosse players." </news/best-sport-for-hedge-fund-job>
People who work for hedge funds tend to be highly competitive and highly disciplined. Kirk McKeown, ex-head of proprietary research at Point72 said that top hedge fund professionals "treat their brains and careers as if they were pro athletes" by effectively managing their physical and mental health in an intense industry. This is particularly important as you progress towards becoming a PM; Will England, CIO of Walleye, said in 2023 that portfolio management jobs are "psychologically extremely toxic" </news/2023/09/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund> by nature, and it "takes a certain sort of psychological profile" to withstand the stress. McKeown said that strategies to maintain mental health can be as small as a daily checklist or as large as having a therapist.
Some skills are more important for juniors than they are for seniors, particularly AI fluency. At Millennium, <https://www.businessinsider.com/millennium-ai-summer-internship-wall-street-hedge-fund-2026-7> all interns are encouraged to use the technology, and the fund has created a special intern track for engineers focused on developing AI solutions. Top candidates in any track are able to build AI tools, and explain how they use them.
Junior traders are also absorbing duties of other support roles; one trader told us </news/quant-researchers-spend-all-their-time-coding-while-junior-traders-do-real-quant-work> young traders today do an increasing amount of complex quant research. He said he needs to "code at a much better standard than junior traders in the past, who only needed to pass Python 101."
It's difficult to break into any of the top graduate schemes; Citadel, Point72, Balyasny and Millennium each accept less than 1% of applicants for their internships. While these numbers can be inflated by subpar applicants, one recruiter told us last year </news/hedge-fund-tech-recruiter-i-sent-500-graduate-c-vs-5-were-accepted?utm_source=chatgpt.com> that only one in 100 graduates with 2.1 STEM degrees from "top tier universities," </news/cfa-mba-caia-phd-or-masters-what-do-hedge-funds-want> actually broke into the industry.
What skills are hedge fund recruiters looking for?
Having the right attitude and personality is all well and good, but if you don't have evidence of those traits you won't get anywhere. Headhunters and recruiters look for specific tangible signals that suggest you have all the wonderful traits above.
One recruiter, speaking anonymously, told us that a track record is the most obvious signal they search for when making external investment hires. "I've yet to meet a fund that doesn't require at least a year's worth of track record," he said. "They want to know what Sharpe ratio you're running at and your holding period horizons." If you're applying for graduate roles, this can be hard to demonstrate, but there are options. You can get involved in your university's investment society, or, if you have the available funds, you can run your own proprietary trading strategy.
An exaggerated track record, however, will set you back. Giorgi De Santis, an ex-Goldman Sachs </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> MD and hedge fund director said in a YouTube video in June <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EhHZ3k4KS4c> that a pet peeve of his is "people who overstate what they achieve" on their CVs. If you interned on a successful trading desk managing $100m in AUM, don't say that you, yourself, were the one managing that money. Wild claims will be interrogated so ensure you have the evidence to back them up.
Ilana Weinstein, a prominent hedge fund recruiter said in 2023 that, <https://ritholtz.com/2023/07/transcript-ilana-weinstein-2/>when hiring portfolio managers, she searches for “risk management, portfolio construction, hedging, sizing, [and] the ability to build and manage a team.” When hiring investment analysts, the focus is instead on "idea generation, creativity, independent research, and asking the right questions."
Return to our guide to hedge fund jobs here. </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>

item.title: Citi hired a Barclays saleswoman in Singapore to build its rates business
item.description:
Shermaine Chia has had a good summer. After nine years at Barclays in Singapore, where she was latterly a senior vice president in G10 rates and FX sales, the Singapore Monetary Authority register shows her leaving the British bank in June.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Now Shermaine Chia has a new job. It's at a US bank instead.
Chia didn't respond to a request to comment for this article, but we understand that her new job is at Citi, where she will be helping to build out the G10 rates business in Asia. Citi declined to comment on this supposition.
Chia is understood to have been a star at Barclays and to have been pursued by banks in the Asian market. It's not clear why she left the British bank.
Macro salespeople are hot in Asia. </news/singapore-macro-hiring>There have been over 30 moves so far this year, most of them involving banks rather than hedge funds, although Franck Wang quietly went from Morgan Stanley to Balyasny in June.
Macro traders are hot too. Morgan Stanley has many gaps to fill. </news/morgan-stanley-s-macro-team-actually-lost-far-more-people-than-we-thought>Sahil Aggarwal </news/sahil-aggarwal-morgan-stanley>, a recently promoted managing director (MD) in rates trading at Morgan Stanley in Singapore, left in June. We are waiting to find out where he's going next.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Repentant private equity firm's new approach to keeping juniors happy. Intense life of 32-year old fintech man
item.description:
Last week a meme was circulating <https://x.com/litcapital/status/2092336758914519378?s=20> concerning the extremely thin cuts of carried interest </news/what-is-carried-interest>that are likely to come your way as a junior in a private equity fund. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> That is, if you get any carried interest at all.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Now, a repentant London private equity fund that formerly had a strategy of inflating the price of a thyroid drug sold to the NHS by 6,000% over a 10-year period, <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2021/jul/30/drug-firm-that-hiked-prices-by-6000-paid-shareholders-400m>is splashing carried interest around to everyone at the fund. Including juniors. Including support staff.
The fund is Cinven. Speaking to the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/f02b04da-c2f4-4a33-adbc-1ee170426207?syn-25a6b1a6=1>Cinven's newly wholesome co-heads declared that they have opened up the pool of Cinven carried interest so that every Cinven employee can wet themselves within it. They are also holding Monday morning investment team meetings, which juniors attend, and at which the damp old dogs are encouraged to explain every aspect of new investments, old investments, and exit processes. “It is hugely appreciated because it helps, especially the more junior people, to get up on the learning curve very quickly,” says one of Cinven's new bosses, whose name is Jorge Quemada.
Quemada and his colleague were appointed in December after Cinven's previous chief executive resigned. He did so after Cinven's earlier methods of earning carried interest were scrutinised. In 2015, Cinven sold a pharmaceutical group for £2.3bn in what the fund described <https://www.ft.com/content/916de087-d197-4743-933e-3454acca834d?syn-25a6b1a6=1>at the time as “one of the most successful deals we’ve ever done.” However, Cinven's successful strategy was subsequently found to have involved ratcheting up the prices of niche pharmaceutical products overlooked by the regulator. Last year, it was fined <https://www.gov.uk/government/news/court-upholds-cmas-99m-fine-on-pharma-over-excessive-nhs-thyroid-drug-prices> £52m.
Times are different now. There is Jorge and there is co-chief executive Bruno Schick. There is a new legal and compliance team of 17 people. The new focus is on collaborating, doing deals, returning cash to investors.
Cinven has been busy hiring juniors and interns from big US banks and top universities. It also has a new inhouse chef with experience of catering for "fine dining." Maybe it will pay more than a sliver of carried interest to employees at the bottom of the pile? Maybe not.
Separately, if you want to work 80 hour weeks for a thrusting man who made millions (maybe hundreds of them) in his late 20s, Alan Chang </news/alan-chang-revolut-fuse> is hiring.
The Times <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/alan-chang-direct-style-fuse-energy-txrvpm7br> says that Chang, who made his money at Revolut, wants to hire 120 people for his new energy company "Fuse" before the year is out. They won't have to work in the office. They will be able to work whenever they want. They won't even need a cover letter when they apply.
Sounds great, except that Chang is the sort of person who - in the words of Kirk McKeown <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=byEXabVAxus>, the former head of research at hedge fund Point72, approaches every day with "rigour." He's single. He doesn't drink. He doesn't watch films. He doesn't read books. He himself is in the office 80-90 hours a week.
Some of Chang's young employees complained to the Observer <https://observer.co.uk/news/business/article/they-milk-them-to-the-max-fuse-energy-accused-of-mistreating-staff> in January that they were being expected to work 100 hour weeks and their lives were miserable. “A lot of people, a lot of companies, they don’t speak the uncomfortable truth,” Chang told the Times. “We have a truth-seeking culture.” Some may enjoy this.
Meanwhile...
EY is investing $100m in rewards for employees who show skills like adaptability, innovation and judgment, as well as experimentation with AI. Individuals can earn spot awards up to $500; teams can earn $25k. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/business/ernst-young-is-giving-100-million-in-bonuses-to-staff-for-human-skills-9320e93d?mod=e2tw>
Alex Gerko made a record £895m from the profits of XTX Markets last year. £1.7bn was shared between Gerko and his quantitative traders and top tech developers. The 23 other people took home £833m between them, an average of £36.2m each. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/c1c79d47-31c0-4e4e-85b6-57527e31d78f?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
The Trump administration just changed internship laws for international students. Now they may only complete internships if employers have a partnership with their school. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/us-news/education/trump-limits-internships-for-international-college-students-5b668796?mod=hp_lead_pos6>
Citadel and Marshall Wace are still battling </news/citadel-marshall-wace> over the recruitment of Adam Shatz who left Citadel to become Marshall Wace's head of credit. Now Citadel wants Marshall Wace to reveal the communications of Anthony Clake and Alpha Plus fund co-PM Alan Hofmeyr, whom it says were involved in hiring Shatz. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/citadel-marshall-wace-recruitment-dan-shatz-legal-battle-2026-8>
Citadel says Marshall Wace was supposed to hand over documents relating to Shatz' recruitment three months ago, but has not done so. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-31/citadel-says-marshall-wace-stonewalling-in-recruitment-spat>
Marshall Wace is opening a Japan office. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-28/marshall-wace-joins-hedge-fund-peers-in-planning-japan-office?taid=6a9122bd1aac0900013263f7&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Yao Hua Ooi helped build a $6.3 billion systematic trading strategy at AQR. Now he's gone to Capula for something similar. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-28/hedge-fund-capula-launches-new-strategy-in-diversification-push?taid=6a91af5d6aa06700017f3cce&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Asian equities are the place to be. BCG Expand estimates Asia Pacific's share of global equities revenues will increase from 21% in 2024 to 25% this year, roughly in line with EMEA. (IFR) <https://www.ifre.com/people-and-markets/2476077/from-backwater-to-driving-force-asia-emerges-as-crucial-equities-trading-hub>
Gavin Yates, head of Arini Capital's US business, has left. So has Ben Elliott in the US team. Arini lost 8% in July. It's not clear why Yates or Elliott left. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-28/arini-s-head-of-us-investments-gavin-yates-leaves-hedge-fund?taid=6a920d1d6aa06700017f4151&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Hedge funds in Brazil are giving up and ceding staff and assets to banks. “We are going through a cyclical downturn for hedge funds, with extremely high interest rates and very strong competition from products that enjoy tax advantages.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-31/brazil-banks-poach-hedge-fund-stars-as-industry-boom-goes-bust?taid=6a958433e7f74f0001fb5fd4&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
A curious business model. Guggenheim controlled four insurance companies in all. Between them, they invested $5.1 billion in debt issued by companies linked to Guggenheim and loaned almost $1 billion to Guggenheim business associates, while also reinsuring each other's risk. (Net Interest) <https://www.netinterest.co/p/untangling-guggenheim?utm_source=substack&publication_id=43559&post_id=213127156&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=8g1t6v&triedRedirect=true#footnote-4>
JPMorgan hired Robin Rousseau from Citi as vice chair. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/jpmorgan-hires-top-citigroup-dealmaker-rousseau-as-m-a-vice-chair-21788c13>
Anthropic is preparing for an enormous IPO after the September 7th Labor Day holiday. Other companies thinking of IPOs are having to work around this and the November mid-terms. Some are deciding it's too much bother. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-31/anthropic-s-mega-ipo-plan-looms-over-packed-us-listing-calendar>
If Reform are elected in the UK, they will have a sovereign wealth fund staffed with people on competitive salaries. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-28/reform-would-pay-city-salaries-to-lure-talent-to-uk-wealth-fund?taid=6a91a4d26aa06700017f3c77&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Working in cybersecurity has become a nightmare in the age of AI. Some in the industry are tinkering with old ham radios and studying the tenets of stoicism to relax. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-31/ai-driven-hacking-boom-fuels-cybersecurity-burnout-at-hospitals-and-banks?taid=6a95787c4f5fab00011024b3&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>

item.title: The ex-JPMorgan & UBS trader helping men through divorce: "It's not a case of winning"
item.description:
If you're a solitary single man in London this bank holiday weekend and are on your own after a divorce, you could always go to Clapham Common on Sunday. Not for a walk or to hang around the bushes, but to meet Photis Kassianides, a former trader who's now an accredited counsellor and divorce coach working with men in financial services.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Kassianides spent nearly three decades in trading, working everywhere from UBS to JPMorgan and Jefferies. In June 2025 he set up Emotional Equity Coaching to help men after divorce and separation. "It's very difficult for men," he says. "I had a great friendship group and supportive extended family, but I still struggled."
Kassianides got divorced from his wife of 20 years in 2019. He had a son aged eight and a daughter aged 11. "I was a senior sales trader and was trying to hold down a new job," he says. "I know what it's like to go through it." In the wake of the divorce, a lot of the struggle came from missing his children.
For a lot of men in financial services, Kassianides says separation and divorce come as a complete surprise. "You have a five to ten year plan. You go to work, you pay for the private schooling, the house, three nice holidays a year and cars. You think you are doing your bit and suddenly it gets blown up. It's very difficult."
Men in banks are often very focused on "powering through" and being a provider, says Kassianides, but they don't always notice the cues that their partners are unhappy. "People are often caught completely unaware," he says. "Their partner will turn around and say, 'You haven't been present and we don't need you.'"
He helps his clients process what went wrong. As they rake over the coals, Kassianides says there are often signs the relationship was fracturing. In some cases, his clients' wives had said explicitly that they were unhappy and had been ignored. In others, there are smaller indications - wives who previously complained about being neglected stopped objecting and didn't seem to notice absences.
Even if male bankers and traders have been travelling often and frequently absent, Kassianides says the disintegration of a family can hit them hard. "It's like a bereavement," he says. "There's a loss of confidence and a loss of identity, with a combination of anger, guilt, fear, shame, regret and loneliness." Living alone without the children is hard.
Kassianides coaches his clients to prevent a spiral into poor mental and physical health: "It's about going to the gym, eating well and getting into good sleep patterns."
He also coaches them to put their children first. "My own divorce happened just before my daughter changed school and she said to me, 'Great timing, dad,'" he recalls. "I was very conscious that they were about to be teenagers and would remember how I'd behaved."
It's easy for people from a highly competitive industry to think that a successful divorce is about winning against a former spouse. Kassianides says this is the wrong way to go about things. "People become antagonistic and competitive and lose track of the damage being done to the children." He counsels his clients to take a step back before responding to things: "Don't send that text or email, or at least send it to me first."
Kassianides is holding his first walk and talk for men, <https://luma.com/gotau55r> most of whom are likely to be from the City, starting from Clapham Common's Windmill pub <https://www.windmillclapham.co.uk/>at 11am this Sunday. There's no charge. "It's for anyone who wants to get out and have a chat with other men," he says. "I know how much I could have done with something like this when I was getting divorced, and how much getting out, moving and talking still helps me now."

item.title: Citi hired a Credit Suisse data guy who left in 2024 and made him MD
item.description:
As we have noted, </news/citi-is-making-cuts-to-its-data-teams-they-may-be-substantial-or-not> Citi is now at least 90% of the way through the work associated with its 2020 regulatory consent order. In possibly related or possibly unrelated developments, Citi has been cutting people in its data teams. </news/citi-is-making-cuts-to-its-data-teams-they-may-be-substantial-or-not>But in London, Citi has made a large hire with a data history.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This large hire is Lee Ellmore, a man with nearly three decades of operations and data expertise, who was last seen at Credit Suisse, which he left in June 2024 according to the FCA Register and his own LinkedIn profile.
Neither Ellmore nor Citi responded to a request to comment for this article, but Ellmore's LinkedIn profile says he's now joining the leadership team for Citi's London markets operations team in a hybrid capacity as an MD. We know no more.
During his long years at Credit Suisse, Ellmore was everything from global head of cash equities middle office to global head of strategic change (including prime) to global head of data, to chief data officer. He knows his stuff.
It's not clear what he's been doing for the past two years. If Ellmore's able to hire at Citi, he possibly has a lot of ex-colleagues who might be interested in finding jobs there too.

item.title: Pay for financial services accountants: could be better
item.description:
How much do accountants </news/accounting-job-finance-banking> earn? Possibly seven-figures, in the right place (such as being a partner at a Big Four firm </news/working-for-the-big-four-pwc-deloitte-ey-kpmg>). In an investment bank, however, pay is much more limited.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
The figures below come from Morgan McKinley’s 2026 UK Salary Calculator <https://www.morganmckinley.com/uk/salary-guide/calculator>. Pay for financial services accountants can range from £50k ($68k) to £200k+ ($272k) depending on seniority. Naturally, more senior professionals with broader responsibilities are paid better than those with narrow ones.
Product control salaries specifically, which follow the analyst through to VP progression quite well, are far behind what even the most junior investment bankers </news/london-bank-analyst-pay> earn in the City.
Pay, interestingly, was not so great in the USA, where it usually much better. The figures below come from Robert Half’s 2026 Finance and Accounting Salaries and Salary Trends <https://www.roberthalf.com/us/en/insights/salary-guide/finance-and-accounting> report. The firm said the highest premiums went to financial professionals with niche transformation talents such as skills in “AI, automation, cybersecurity, cloud engineering and data analytics.”
However, there is a disconnect between what employers are willing to offer and what candidates want. Robert Half said that 80% of hiring managers are concerned about “keeping pace with candidates’ pay expectations.” Yes, for the figures below.
In our 2026 Compensation & Lifestyle Report </banking-compensation-guide>, we found that support function professionals in financial services reported salaries between $40k and $300k on average a year depending on seniority, and bonuses between $10k and $110k on average, again depending on seniority.
But the big benefit of working in support roles is the work-life balance </news/finance-best-lifestyle>. Our report also found that finance professionals worked just 42 hours a week on average – well below their peers in investment banking, for example, who worked for 62 hours a week on average.

item.title: Morning Coffee: The eccentric guy running Jane Street. Citi's banker comings and Citi's banker goings
item.description:
It was already well known </news/jpmorgan-cut-junior-bankers-ai> that Rob Granieri, the 53-year-old billionaire running Jane Street, is not like Jamie Dimon, the 70-year-old billionaire running JPMorgan or David Solomon, the 64-year-old multimillionaire running Goldman Sachs. Granieri is younger; he has hair down to his waist; he likes Metallica and attends Burning Man. Dimon and Solomon are uptight in his shade. Granieri is probably not a fan of euphoric house music. </news/david-solomon-goldman-sachs>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As Jane Street succumbs to scrutiny in the wake of its $15bn loss in July </news/jane-street-12bn-loss>, Granieri is in the limelight. This time <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-10-02/jane-street-billionaire-rob-granieri-smashes-wall-street-trading-records>he is not dancing in a shiny jacket and fedora.
Described last year by Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-10-02/jane-street-billionaire-rob-granieri-smashes-wall-street-trading-records> as a shy introvert and the sort of person you might encounter on a park bench reading Shakespeare, Granieri is the centre of Jane Street's universe, says the Financial Times. <https://www.ft.com/content/ea9c073d-4e9d-4e8a-98c0-68e278faa081?emailId=c7e6c715-9613-4871-a82d-dc80a9b326f2&segmentId=22011ee7-896a-8c4c-22a0-7603348b7f22&syn-25a6b1a6=1>“As much as they like to pretend he’s not the guy, he’s the guy,” one person familiar with Jane Street told the FT. There's no CEO at Jane Street, but Granieri is the last of the four founders still at the firm. Persons told the FT he is Jane Street personified.
Despite this, Granieri doesn't seem to be standing up in front of his people and giving motivational townhall speeches. People at the firm apparently don't all know who he is. Sometimes they speak to him without comprehending his centrality. When Jane Street lost the $15bn someone called Turner Batty </news/jane-street-12bn-loss>messaged the Jane Street staff to point out that it had been a "bad month."
Granieri is not, however, without some flexes. When it's a company dinner, the FT says he might order steak for dessert. Or he might order the whole meal again. He likes fine dining. He likes to eat at Le Bernardin in New York. His parents ran a banquet hall called Chateau Granieri in Norristown Pennsylvania.
Bloomberg reported previously that Granieri was careful with his early career. He was offered a job cold-calling and pitching stocks but he turned that down. He got a job at Susquehanna International Group after printing out resumes and dropping them off at tall buildings in Pennsylvania. He was making $700k at SIG aged 27, but he didn't like a middle manager there and so he left and founded Jane Street instead with two colleagues and one other.
Those colleagues were Mike Jenkins and Tim Reynolds. Reynolds was nearly paralyzed in a crash <https://spinalcordinjuryzone.com/news/2477/paralyzed-man-donates-1m> after a Jane Street party and left Jane Street in 2012. Reynolds now runs private resorts. <https://aniprivateresorts.com/>Jenkins left and walks a pot-bellied pig in a Manhattan park.
Only Granieri is still around. Bloomberg said he avoids long vacations and stays online until odd hours. Sometimes he buys a smart outfit for a client meeting. The FT says he is an oddball with a formidable intellect. He likes casinos and Jane Street's trading floor has been gamified with animal noises and more. Other people seem to like this too. “It’s just recruiting,” one former Jane Street employee told the FT. “They hire the best people in the world for what they do and they don’t fuck that up.”
Sounds great. Granieri isn't immune to mistakes though. He was once conned by a former nun <https://www.reuters.com/article/markets/ex-nun-ordered-to-pay-1-mln-for-milking-mississippi-casino-deal-idUSL1N0YI1RR/> with lavish spending habits. He was once duped into funding an alleged coup <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-06-25/jane-street-s-rob-granieri-says-he-was-duped-into-funding-south-sudan-coup-plot> in South Sudan. He is partial to 24-year-old hedge fund wunderkind Leopold Aschenbrenner and attended Aschenbrenner's big wedding earlier this month. Jane Street also invested $2.5bn in Aschenbrenner's fund. The $2.5bn became $10bn and then shrunk to $3bn in July. Granieri is still up. It may be too early to have a steak dessert to celebrate.
Separately, Citi needs more bankers because Citi says </news/citi-investor-day-2026> it has 100 fewer managing directors than rival banks at the 75th centile of its "core peer group".
Citi has been hiring some new MDs, but it's also been losing them. Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-hires-hsbc-banker-dixit-for-media-deals-6896b4fa>says Citi hired Bhavin Dixit, a technology media and telecoms (TMT) banker </news/highest-paid-bankers> at HSBC in London who weirdly survived last year's HSBC cull. This follows the hiring of five other TMT bankers <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/citigroup-hires-five-us-tech-investment-banking-executives-rivals-2026-07-22/> in the US and various hires from Deutsche Bank </news/citi-hiring-deutsche-bank> and elsewhere.
However, Citi is leaking bankers too. In the US, Dan McDow has gone to JPMorgan <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/jpmorgan-hiring-citigroups-mcdow-run-east-coast-tech-investment-bank-memo-says-2026-08-25/>to run East Coast M&A. In London, TMT banker Robert Farrington left in May. Also in London, head of asset management M&A Hamish Summerfield is off to Perella Weinberg.
Revenues in Citi's M&A business were up only 7.4% in the first half of this year. That compared to over 60% at Bank of America, Barclays and Morgan Stanley. The implication is that Citi is losing market share. It may need to hire some more bankers yet.
Meanwhile...
Citadel Securities tripled its trading revenues to $7.3bn and made $2.2bn of income. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-27/citadel-securities-notches-record-7-3-billion-trading-haul?taid=6a90cd330d091100013ebb87&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Dorothee Blessing, the co-head of investment banking at JPMorgan, says she's hiring bankers too, particularly for technology, healthcare and financial sponsors teams. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/jpmorgans-dealmaking-boss-blessing-were-not-standing-still-7e38d2f1?mod=homepage>
Millennium wanted to hire Tang Lin, a portfolio manager from Dymon Asia. She accepted a job offer. Then she changed her mind. Now Millennium wants $2.5m to cover its costs of preparing to hire her. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-27/millennium-sues-dymon-trader-for-2-5-million-after-gazumping?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>
Simon Costello was a senior FX options trader at Goldman Sachs. He left for hedge fund Balyasny and worked there for nine months before returning to Goldman. (IFR) <https://www.ifre.com/people-and-markets/2476066/moves-fx-trader-costello-returns-to-goldman>
The coroner found that the UK Treasury “materially contributed” to the death of a 26-year-old personal assistant who took her own life after facing disciplinary proceedings. She attended an informal meeting and then had her job responsibilities temporarily changed and her access to the diary of her manager removed. She was convinced she was going too lose her job, even though this wasn't the case. (BBC) <https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/aug/10/treasury-materially-contributed-to-suicide-of-personal-assistant-chloe-moffat-coroner-finds>
Consultants want everyone back in the office because they say AI made interpersonal skills more valuable. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/7fd9c234-a92b-4ab2-ba1f-969cf9a23f52?emailId=c7e6c715-9613-4871-a82d-dc80a9b326f2&segmentId=22011ee7-896a-8c4c-22a0-7603348b7f22&syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Jes Staley is surprised about Jeffrey Epstein. “You know, you can go to jail for . . . a year and you’ve been convicted of abusing minors, it’s just incredible to me that he would continue to do it after he got out of jail.” (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/5250dd00-5bfc-44ce-80d6-2295c020efb8?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Stephen Miran declares the US treasury market is fine. "The recent increase in bond yields is therefore almost entirely due to higher expected overnight rates over the long term. In other words, investors are marking up their expectations for long-run economic growth, not becoming concerned over central bank or fiscal credibility. The market could be recognising that AI, deregulation and better tax policy are turbocharging the American economy." (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/a919761d-dab1-4a6e-93fe-f69910192c1c>

item.title: “I was on the board of a bank. My colleagues ruined my career”
item.description:
I am writing this article from the embers of my career in banking. I know financial services. It’s an industry I worked in for my whole career. But I have become unemployable.
My fall is something to be studied and learned from. I am writing this anonymously and I don’t want to reveal my identity. Although I was a big fee earner in my area, I rose to the top of a bank by running a function that was not a major revenue generator. I was on the board, but I had no power. The revenue generators ran the show.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The firm I worked for had issues and was struggling. As an insider, I could see this very clearly. My colleagues on the board were pursuing strategies that I thought made no sense and that in my opinion were inappropriate for a regulated company. We were embroiled in discrimination cases and were desperate for external funding.
Eventually, I told the regulator. I became a whistleblower and the case was very slowly investigated. While this was occurring, the bank’s financial situation worsened and I was made redundant.
I took the bank to court and I won a nominal but not a lifechanging amount of money. For reasons that I cannot share, I could not get the additional settlements usually offered to whistleblowers.
The stress made me seriously ill. I took time out for my own health. I didn’t tell anyone in the industry about my experiences at the bank, or about the fact that I was pursuing a whistleblowing claim with the regulator. I didn’t want to be considered a troublemaker.
Meanwhile, many of my former colleagues found new jobs. Most are now employed in senior roles elsewhere on high salaries. </banking-compensation-guide> I have found myself in the opposite situation. I have been blacklisted </news/2010/02/beware-the-unofficial-city-blacklist>and am locked out of the market. It seems incredibly unfair. Things that occurred after I left showed that my complaints were valid, and the regulator eventually confirmed this. Again, I cannot share details.
The moral of my story is that it pays to say nothing. As was written here last week </news/career-advice-banking>, it makes sense to keep your head down. If you don’t, you will be punished. None of my former colleagues should be employed in my opinion. And yet, here we are.

item.title: One of the 'finest boys in finance' has left Goldman Sachs
item.description:
When your name and face become infamous </news/goldman-sachs-junior-bankers-magazine-shoot> across the sector in which you work, it can be prudent to look for a change of scenery. Mason Clarke, an investment banker in the entertainment team at Goldman Sachs </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs>, became a bit too well known by his peers after a viral profile on him and other young finance professionals appeared in Interview Magazine <https://www.interviewmagazine.com/fashion/meet-the-finest-boys-in-finance> earlier this year. The publication declared him one of the 'Finest Boys in Finance.' </news/demarre-johnson>A few months on, he is in finance no more.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Clarke has now joined football (soccer) club Inter Miami, moving to Miami for the role. He joins as an investments and development associate for the club and its multi-purpose venue, the Nu Stadium. Clarke spent the last two years at Goldman in New York after joining as a graduate. The circumstances of his departure are unclear, but his last day at the firm was the 20th of August according to his FINRA BrokerCheck profile. Goldman Sachs declined to comment.
Clarke was one of four young professionals profiled by Interview, and one of two to come from Goldman Sachs. The other, Clay Nelson, is an associate in its markets division and, according to FINRA, remains with the bank. There was some speculation that the pair would be sanctioned following the interviews; a Goldman spokesperson told the New York Post <https://nypost.com/2026/03/05/business/baby-faced-goldman-sachs-bankers-could-be-fired-over-unauthorized-magazine-photo-shoots-sources/> in March that their interviews were not cleared internally, but Nelson continuing at the firm suggests that the most they received was a slap on the wrist.
Clarke is not the first of the Finest Boys in Finance to leave their job. Demarre Johnson, an AI analyst at PwC, left the consulting firm </news/demarre-johnson-finest-boys-in-finance>prior to the release of the profiles. You could argue that he wasn't technically in finance to begin with, but he has ironically entered the industry despite the backlash; he told us in June </news/demarre-johnson> that he now works for a hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>. Johnson told us that he "became a name" on the street, was frequently approached by waves of "random finance bros" and was accosted by women trying to date him. It's unclear whether Clarke, who did not respond to a request for comment, had similar experiences.
When faced with that kind of infamy, taking a job outside of New York makes sense, and Miami seems like the obvious place to go given the efforts of Citadel and other hedge funds to make the city 'Wall Street South.' </news/hedge-funds-are-following-citadel-to-miami-they-re-disappointed-in-the-tech-talent> Clarke will presumably miss the "energy, hustle and grit" of New York. He presumably won't miss the rats.

item.title: Ex-Citadel partner's new $1bn London hedge fund got off to a flying start
item.description:
Agave Capital Management, the macro hedge fund </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund> of ex-Citadel </news/2022/10/how-to-get-a-job-at-citadel> PM and partner Gilberto Marcheggiano, was one of the bigger launches in 2025. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-07-10/ex-citadel-portfolio-manager-joins-rare-1-billion-launch-club> reported that the London-based fund </news/best-paying-hedge-funds>launched in July with $1bn (£736m) in assets under management (AUM). Last week, it filed accounts with the UK's Companies House that suggest its early months went very well.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
'Agave Capital Management Limited' just released accounts from November 2024 (pre-launch) to the end of 2025. Agave is paying people handsomely. It employed 20 people on average during the period covered by the accounts and paid an average of £291.8k ($397k) in 'salaries and wages' for the 13 months. Many of its employees joined in May, or later, so the annual pay rate is likely to be much higher than this.
Marcheggiano has been hiring some old colleagues. Before Citadel, he was head of cross macro investments at Goldman Sachs. In March 2026, he hired Giancarlo Ferrero, another former Goldman fixed income PM with whom he also worked at Citadel. In February, Marcheggiano hired Benjamin Nelson, a senior economist and ex-Balyasny director, with whom he worked at the Bank of England early in his career.
Over the 13 month period covered by the accounts, Agave recorded a turnover of £21m ($28.5m) all in the form of 'investment management fees.' Agave's accounts state that this is a mix of both monthly management fees and performance fees that are recognized when returns crystallize.
Agave did not respond to a request for comment. The accounts show that the fund was owed £14.3m in 'prepayments and accrued income' at the end of the year, though this isn't broken down between management fees and performance fees. If we assume a substantial portion of this (£10m or more) reflects crystallized gains, that might suggest mid-single digit returns for investors on an AUM of $1bn.
Some of the biggest fund launches in recent memory, including Jain Global </news/jain-global-hedge-fund-jobs> and ExodusPoint, posted returns of less than 1% in their first half-year of operations. </news/jain-global-exoduspoint#:~:text=During%20its%20first%20half%20year%20of%20operation%2C%20ExodusPoint%20generated%20returns%20of%200.57%25%2C%20only%20slightly%20higher%20than%20Jain%27s%200.5%25.%20In%202022%2C%20ExodusPoint%20suffered%20%24400m%2B%20of%20redemptions%2C%20followed%20by%20another%20%241bn%20in%20the%20first%20half%20of%202024.%20But%20now%20look.%C2%A0>

item.title: How AI is changing accounting jobs in finance
item.description:
Artificial intelligence is impacting the entire financial services industry. Accounting and audit </news/accounting-job-finance-banking> functions are no different, and as the pace of technological growth continues, these functions might end up being some of the most completely overhauled. But what does that look like in practice?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
To start with, AI is absorbing many of the tasks through which junior accountants traditionally learned the job. Big four firm Deloitte, for example, is overhauling graduate training <https://www.icaew.com/insights/viewpoints-on-the-news/2026/mar-2026/how-deloitte-is-reshaping-its-audit-training-for-the-ai-age> in its UK audit and assurance business from September 2026; trainees will now sit 12 out of 14 exams in their first year of practice (the exams were formerly spread over three years). Deloitte UK Managing Partner for Audit and Assurance Allee Bonnard told the ICAEW <https://www.icaew.com/insights/viewpoints-on-the-news/2026/mar-2026/how-deloitte-is-reshaping-its-audit-training-for-the-ai-age> that the new program will lead to stronger “communication, teamwork and problem solving” skills rather than focusing just on “old-school accounting”, such as performing a cash reconciliation. The supposition is that this old-school work can now be done by AI.
Inside banks, the same logic applies. Product control's daily P&L production, financial control's reconciliations, and the first draft of almost any report are exactly the sort of workloads that AI tools can now handle instead of a human being.
When we looked at the day in the life of a Deloitte banking and capital markets auditor </news/day-in-the-life-deloitte> Bella Smith, she noted that AI was providing “some initial analysis” which she further refined (and checked, of course). “The technology helps us to understand movements… that may have previously been harder to spot,” she said.
Deloitte’s Bonnard said that accounting will become “more engaging and exciting” in the future. How that works, and how it will work in the future, varies significantly between firms – KPMG said last year <https://kpmg.com/uk/en/about/our-impact/report-hub/transparency/audit-quality.html> that its AI agent, Clara, was for “flowcharting”, as well as easily finding documentation from previous years.
Tedious but necessary work, essentially, but with a rather material impact on hiring - Deloitte's own UK early-careers intake fell from more than 1,700 in 2023 <https://www.deloitte.com/uk/en/about/press-room/seventeen-hundred-graduates-and-apprentices-start-their-careers-at-deloitte.html> to less than 1,500 in 2025 <https://www.deloitte.com/uk/en/about/press-room/deloitte-welcomes-next-generation-of-talent.html>, for example.
The exact headcount impact this will have at banks is unclear, but given how banks treat their middle- and back-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> teams, no doubt many roles will go the way of the dodo. Banks including ABN Amro, Unicredit, BNP Paribas, and others </news/morgan-stanley-ai-banking-jobs> plan to reduce headcount specifically in support functions due to AI. Financial roles like accounting are very much in that bucket.
On top of how existing jobs are changing, a new generation of startups is going further and building their operating models around the use of AI. Repodo, an audit firm founded by former executives of Nordic neobank Lunar (and a professional auditor), raised €8.2m in pre-seed funding in August 2026 in Denmark, Finextra reported <https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48303/ex-lunar-founders-raise-82m-to-launch-ai-native-audit-firm-repodo>. It automates data collection, reconciliations, documentation, and transaction analysis, while human auditors provide the risk assessments, professional judgements, and sign-off.
It’s not the only one. Berlin-based Cortea raised €12m in June, EU-Strartups reported <https://www.eu-startups.com/2026/06/berlin-based-cortea-raises-e12-million-seed-round-to-build-ai-quality-layer-for-audit-firms/>, backed by former KPMG global head of audit Larry Bradley. Cortea builds AI agents that review reports and financial statements before human auditors sign them off. It says its agents managed to get through more than 4,000 audit reports in a single season, flagging issues in every one. It’s unclear if these were particularly bad reports.
However, AI doesn't remove the need for the qualification altogether, and seemingly it won’t any time soon. The Financial Reporting Council said <https://www.frc.org.uk/news-and-events/news/2026/03/innovative-new-guidance-supports-audit-firm-adoption-of-emerging-ai-technologies/> in March guidance that "the human auditor is always accountable" for audit outputs, no matter how much of the work the tools perform. UK company law still requires a named senior statutory auditor to sign the report in their own name. Deloitte’s skills of the future - “strong communication, teamwork and problem solving” - will need to be supported by traditional skills, too. For the time being.

item.title: How to get an operations job in banking and finance
item.description:
Operations deals with the core “plumbing” systems upon which financial services relies. Operations jobs are dedicated to ensuring the efficiency and the accuracy of each element of a transaction.
Operations jobs have traditionally been seen as less prestigious than the “front-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>” client-facing jobs like M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> or sales and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>. However, this is an increasingly outdated way of thinking about how banks work.
Rodney Sunada-Wong, a former chief risk officer at Morgan Stanley’s broker dealer business, says banks are like a human organism. In Sunada-Wong’s schema, senior management, risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank> and finance </news/accounting-job-finance-banking> are the brain. Salespeople, traders </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>, and investment bankers </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process> are the muscles. Technology </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank> is the skeleton and bones. Treasury is the lungs. And the operations division is the heart and circulatory system.
“All the parts have to work together,” says Sunada-Wong. “The better and more efficient your operations, the more profitable, and efficient your bank will be.” Banks recognize this, and getting operations right is increasingly important for profitability.
The nature of your job in operations will depend upon the area of the banking business that you support. For example, if you work in securities operations and support the trading floor your role will involve the settlement, clearance, and reconciliation (checking that buyers’ and sellers’ documentation match up) processes associated with all the traded instruments (e.g., equities or bonds). But, if you work in loan operations, you’ll be involved with all the administrative processes associated with the lending business from the time loan proceeds are dispersed to the borrower until the loan is repaid.
Similarly, investment banking operations jobs help with the running of the M&A and capital markets functions. Retail banking operations jobs are concerned with transactions involving individuals and are usually carried out at bank branches. Operations jobs can also be known as “back-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> jobs.” In other words, you won’t be dealing with clients directly.
Operations jobs can be harder to get than you'd imagine. Data from Trackr last year </news/hardest-internships-in-banking>, which tracked students attempting to enter the financial services industry, found that the average student applicant to a middle- or back-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> (which includes operations) internship had a success rate of 1.4%, which was tougher than sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> (1.5%) or quant finance </news/quant-jobs-finance> (1.8%)
If you want to work in operations, you have a number of options available to you.
Operations jobs in securities businesses
If you work in an operations job in a securities business, you’ll be supporting the trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> floor. You might be working on:
Clearing: Updating accounts of trading counterparties, matching “buys” and “sells”, and arranging for settlement (ie. payment).
Settlement: Exchanging money and securities between the seller and the buyer on the trade settlement date.
Trade confirmations: Documenting the specific commercial terms of a transaction to which the parties agreed, including pricing.
Reconciliation: Ensuring that the “buys” match the “sells”, resolving errors, or checking the validity of transactions. Operations jobs in banks are about monitoring existing processes and procedures. They’re also about creating improvements and increasing efficiency. In the U.S., most are sponsored by their companies to sit for the Series 7 and Series 63 securities exams.
For a long time, securities operations jobs were the most numerous in investment banks. There were far more people processing transactions on the trading floor than working in sales and trading. These days, much of what happens in the operations division is now controlled by technology, but human beings are still needed to help with exceptions when processes don’t run smoothly. Those humans might not be in London or New York. Securities operations jobs are typically located away from large, expensive financial cities, in places where premises and people are usually less costly like Poland </news/cantor-fitzgerald-hiring-warsaw> or India </news/office-politics-bank-india>.
If you have a job in commodities operations, you’ll carry out many of the same processes as in securities operations – but you’ll also have to deal with the idiosyncrasies of the commodities markets. People with jobs in physical commodities operations need an understanding of what’s involved in buying or selling an actual barrel of oil, for example.
Loan operations jobs
Loan operations jobs ensure the accurate and timely operations of a bank’s loan process. This includes booking loans on the loan system, maintaining loan documents, verifying and auditing key data elements (including financial, tax, and business information, assembling and maintaining credit files on borrowers) managing loan collateral, exception resolution, and performing regulatory reporting. The loan operations function also performs loan research to resolve problems associated with borrowers or transactions, and processes loan payoffs.
Loan operations managers design and administer procedures and systems. They also ensure that each stage of the loan process is carried out in accordance with federal, state, and local laws and regulations, particularly in consumer loans where errors can be very costly.
Investment banking operations jobs
Investment banking operations jobs are about helping the front-office complete M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> and underwriting </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> transactions. If you work in investment banking operations, you might be involved in the due diligence surrounding a deal or working on the graphics of a pitchbook.
In capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> operations, your job will involve supporting the debt capital markets and equity capital markets units as they underwrite the launch of new securities. You’ll assist in data analysis, data presentation, documentation and due diligence and will ensure that the transaction proceeds smoothly. In many ways, your job will be similar to that of securities operations professionals – you’ll be expected to work on client onboarding, trade capture, settlement and clearance, and general client support.
Skills you’ll need for operations jobs in banks
Read More: The skills you need for a career in financial services operations </news/skills-needed-operations>
Operations professionals need strong product and industry knowledge to facilitate transactions and address any processing problems.
They also need to be strong communicators, and capable of dealing with everyone from traders to auditors to investment bankers and need to describe complex processes in simple terms. They also deal extensively with other control functions, including compliance, credit, risk, and technology.
Technical skills are also a critical part of the operations skillset: operational processes are now controlled by complex technology systems and even if operations professional are not coding these systems yourself, they’ll need to understand them. That includes acting as a quarterback for AI agents that are increasingly doing their jobs.
Careers in operations can progress along several different paths. Many professionals find that they are called upon to broaden the scope of their activities as they progress. Others become specialists in a particular aspect of the operations process like settlement, clearance or project management.
How AI is changing operations jobs
Read More: AI’s impact on operations has been brutally efficient </news/ai-in-operations>
Of all the fields of financial services, operations might have been one of the worst exposed to the rising capabilities of artificial intelligence. JPMorgan last year forecast a roughly 10% decline in operations headcount over the next five years, with AI increasingly handling routine processes. Marianne Lake, who made the announcement, even said that 10% was a conservative figure.
The profession also faces pressure to become faster. The UK, EU and Switzerland move to T+1 settlement in October 2027, meaning that trades must be settled one day after they are made, rather than the currently typical two. This leaves operations teams less time to identify and correct errors, and AI agents may increasingly be suited to this speed-sensitive work.
Finally, automation threatens traditional operations hubs such as India, Poland and parts of the US. BNY is already using AI “digital employees” for tasks such as payment validation, shifting human operators towards supervising and training automated systems rather than performing routine processes themselves. Operations employees in low-cost centres will be at risk of job losses.
Education & qualifications you’ll need for operations jobs in banking
Read More: The qualifications you need to work in banking, trading, and more </news/best-qualifications-for-banking-jobs>
Operations professionals are very different to other people in financial services that work closer to the money, and they therefore have different educational requirements. Basically – fewer specifics and requirements for degree topics and the likes.
When we analyzed the junior ranks of Goldman Sachs’ operations team for example, there was an extremely varied range of graduate backgrounds, with law, economics, history, business, and management science all represented.
In the past, financial services firms have recruited a wide variety of people for their operations positions - hedge fund DE Shaw, for instance, is known to have hired painters and poets </news/2023/08/de-shaw-hedge-fund-hiring-painters-poets>. Fine arts masters aside, there’s also the Investment Operations Certificate (IOC) from CISI, although it’s primarily a UK-recognized qualification. It can also feed into CISI’s global operations management qualification, a Level 6 diploma, which is hypothetically equivalent to a bachelors degree.
Salaries & bonuses in financial services operations
Read More: Pay for financial services operations people is better than you think </news/compensation-in-operations-finance>
Operations professionals are not paid very well compared to their peers in the front-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>. This is because they are far from revenue generation – they are not bringing in paying clients. Additionally, unlike their peers in compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance> or risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank>, they have a relatively process-driven role.
Generally, the operations professionals still working the United States are best paid. We found that they could earn up to $450k in total compensation, compared to $197k and $150k for senior professionals in Poland and India, respectively.
Our 2026 Compensation & Lifestyle Report </banking-compensation-guide> found that not only do operations professionals earn the least of their peers per hour worked </news/finance-best-lifestyle> ($56), they also earn the least outright - $133k on average, compared to $313k on average in finance and $163k for control & support staff, on average.

item.title: An ex-JPMorgan MD is hiring traders at OpenAI
item.description:
If you work for OpenAI, you might become very rich. The company is planning an IPO for 2027 and was last valued at $852bn. The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/aa0ca006-5af4-4f94-9789-3e56f9f53e1d?syn-25a6b1a6=1> notes that OpenAI handed out nearly $11bn in equity pay to its 8,000 staff in 2024 and 2025 alone. And in May, the WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/tech/openai-employee-stock-sales-71ed10bd > reported that 600 current and former employees of the company sold their shares for $6.6bn and called OpenAI jobs “the greatest lottery ticket of the AI boom.”
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Some people from banks already hold these great lottery tickets. People like Tahreem Kampton. Until April 2026, Kampton was a managing director (MD) in JPMorgan’s treasury team. Now he’s the treasurer at OpenAI. And in this new manifestation, Kampton is hiring.
OpenAI is looking for a head of treasury markets <https://openai.com/careers/head-of-treasury-markets-san-francisco/> to work on Kampton's team. The role was opened in the past few days and pays up to $295k, plus equity. The ideal candidate will have 12 years' experience "across investment management, corporate treasury, capital markets, banking, asset management, interest rate risk management, complex capital structures, credit markets, or related finance roles." Strong modelling skills, strong communication skills and an understanding of hedging and risk management are also a clear plus.
Joining the the OpenAI treasury team could be an interesting business. In 2025, OpenAI generated $13bn in revenues and made a $20bn loss. The company has famously enormous and complex debt obligations of up to $1 trillion <https://www.ftadviser.com/content/4508c52e-6cdb-4384-937e-075316543668https://www.ftadviser.com/content/4508c52e-6cdb-4384-937e-075316543668> involving partner companies financing the construction of its infrastructure.
This might sound like fun if you're the sort of person that can hedge liquidity exposures "where rate movements can create material financial volatility." Maybe you'll get hundreds of millions of dollars of stock if you succeed.
Follow me on X <https://x.com/MadameButcher>. Follow me on LinkedIn. <https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarahbutcherjournalist/>

item.title: Morning Coffee: How precocious 24-year-old hedge fund managers talk at parties. The Russian traders who made a fortune for themselves
item.description:
If someone says “I’m thinking about buying a galaxy <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/situational-awareness-leopold-aschenbrenner-ai-fund-4dbb00a4?mod=hp_lead_pos7>”, most of us would probably reply something like “solid choice <https://www.samsung.com/uk/smartphones/galaxy-s26/buy/?modelCode=SM-S942BZKGEUB&cid=UK_PPC_6818415937_ID~B0009W6G_CN~FeedScore-+High+Potential_BS~mx_SB~smart_PR~smrcro_CH~shop_AT~pmax_OB~conv_PH~on_PK~roah_FS~hld2c_MK~gb_MD~h_PB~gads_PL~goads_FF~-&ad=&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23931934694&gbraid=0AAAAAD8U7YFy7svsdcqoPwHx6quryxOqV&gclid=Cj0KCQjwnbrUBhDOARIsAKKhPpeik92HUaJg3ATQUPcT_SDnAK6mexZ8D99OYC1xKeqiCVDOiOJuiYsaAiixEALw_wcB> but you can get an iPhone for nearly the same money”. If you’re at a party in Silicon Valley, though, it’s just as likely that you’re talking to somebody like Situational Awareness founder Leopold Aschenbrenner, </news/citadel-leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness>who actually does want to buy a galaxy.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Or possibly more than one galaxy, in order to “make his mark on the universe”, as 24-year-old Aschenbrenner has apparently said at several parties. The media coverage does not record how he might have dealt with follow-up questions like “what would you do with one if you owned it?”, “do you know what a light year is, and how long it takes to travel 25,000 of them <https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/features/cosmic/nearest_galaxy_info.html>” or even “there’s already a website <https://wpo.net/galaxies/index.html> that lets you do that, it only costs $19.95”.
We have all met people like this; they seem to be particularly drawn to the investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> industry as well as to tech. People who are very clearly, very obviously incredibly intelligent – Aschenbrenner went to Columbia University at the age of 15, graduated as valedictorian and was described by professors as “one of the most brilliant undergraduates they ever met”.
But, people whose intelligence and original thinking seem to regularly lead them to do and say things which are … kind of dumb. Not just dumb in the “ignoring both the legal reality of ownership and general relativity” kind of way, but also dumb in the “making horrible career moves” kind of way. Aschenbrenner seems to have been one of those.
One might have said that it wasn’t really his fault that his first job out of university was with FTX – plenty of otherwise street-smart people were also taken in by Sam Bankman-Fried, and he got out early (apparently after an unrelated argument with Sam). But when he walked into his next job, at OpenAI, it didn’t take him long to get involved in the internal drama, pick the wrong side and get fired (with a cloud of accusations and counter-accusations about sensitive company information).
And then he sat down and wrote a 160 page blog post, <https://situational-awareness.ai/>called “Situational Awareness”, which was so good that people gave him, at the age of 24, his own $45bn hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>to manage. Which he then levered up by a factor of three, “hedging” his long positions in AI stocks with short positions in stocks that he thought would be vulnerable to AI. In other words, doubling up the same investment thesis rather than de-risking it. Which brings us roughly up to date.
People like this are fascinating company, and they will never be poor for long, because they keep getting job offers. But the lack of common sense can make them somewhat exhausting to be around, particularly if any of your own financial security or wellbeing depends on their judgement. If you ever wonder why investment banking is such a heavily regulated industry, guys like this are a big part of the reason.
Elsewhere, when life hands you lemons, make lemonade. Or, as they might have said in the Luxembourg office of Gazprombank <https://www.ft.com/content/3cb40de7-89f5-4c64-b769-70da374dcd4a?syn-25a6b1a6=1>, when life hands you sanctions, make sanctionsade.
It was quite a simple trade; in the aftermath of the invasion of Ukraine, a lot of Gazprom’s foreign currency debt was “stranded”, in the sense that although the company wasn’t subject to sanctions itself, most of the financial institutions involved in handling its interest payments were, so it became extremely difficult for non-Russian holders to get paid. For this reason, the bonds traded at a hefty discount.
Vladimir Putin’s government decided to solve the problem by allowing them all to be exchanged for new rouble-denominated bonds, held in Russia at full face value. So if you were a Russian citizen who was able to predict which bonds were about to be exchanged, and you had an employer who was willing to lend you lots of money, you could get rich.
It seems a bit too good to be true, and indeed, the news story is full of people “denying all wrongdoing” and pointing to regulatory investigations which didn’t end in action. All four bankers have now left Gazprombank and are doing other things, presumably with fond memories of the day that an opportunity crossed their desk.
Meanwhile …
Deutsche Bank’s cloud computing partnership with Google is extending into using Gemini agents for its lending business – it now has quasi-autonomous AI analysts doing credit risk assessments and portfolio monitoring. These will apparently be extensively deployed later this year, with as yet unspecified consequences for hiring and firing. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-08-26/google-s-gemini-ai-is-changing-how-deutsche-bank-assesses-credit-risk>)
A recent SpaceX job ad isn’t just for someone who knows how to procure the natural gas to power their datacentres – it’s asking for expertise “P&L generation, pricing inefficiencies and CFTC compliance”, which sounds much more like a trading desk role. (Navnoor Bawa Research <https://www.navnoorbawaresearch.com/p/spacex-is-hiring-a-gas-trader-with?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>)
If you didn’t get an offer after a summer internship, </news/internship-investment-bank> it’s a better idea to get feedback quickly and then concentrate on making applications, rather than trying to network. Apparently bankers are a bit disconcerted to be asked for “pick your brains” coffee meetings with students in October. You might have to accept a slightly less glamorous role or location though. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/wall-street-interns-return-offer-advice-2026-8>)
In America, lots of banks have reacted to the shift in political and economic priorities by opening up or growing their Washington DC offices to be close to decision makers. The small but proud investment banking community in Manchester is hoping for a similar effect from Andy Burnham’s “Number 10 North”. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/investment-banks-in-manchester-prepare-for-boost-from-burnham-power-shift-19386254?mod=homepage>)
A Danish start-up is hoping to do what everyone would love to see, but which everyone is scared to try – using AI to automate the drudgery of audit work. The trouble is, you can’t yet automate the work of taking the blame. (Finextra <https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48303/ex-lunar-founders-raise-82m-to-launch-ai-native-audit-firm-repodo>)
A famous clown school in France has proved to be so good at giving people a new lease of life after mid-career burnouts that drama professors are having to warn that it’s not therapy – it’s clowning. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/where-do-aspiring-actors-go-to-cure-burnout-clown-school-ea67571b?mod=mhp>)
